transcript:
Meeting Header:
- Date/Time: 2025-09-10 14:30 UTC
- Duration: ~62 minutes
- Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Marco Alvarez (Redwood), Sofia Tran (Redwood); Lisa Chen (Nimbus ML), Arjun Patel (Nimbus Infra), Emily Rogers (CTO), Samir Khatri (SRE)

Auto Summary (auto-generated, may be rough):
Redwood and Nimbus dug into GPU runtime profiling: kernel scheduler behavior, CUDA graph stability under long prompt/large KV cache conditions, and practical differences observed between TensorRT-LLM (TRT-LLM) and vLLM styles of execution. Key risks discussed: CUDA graph instability when kernels are JITed differently across devices, memory fragmentation causing OOMs on longer sequences, and eviction/backpressure patterns with KV cache. Consensus to run targeted stability matrix and a short Dedicated canary.

Topics Covered:
- Kernel scheduler heuristics and how Redwood's runtime chooses kernels
- CUDA graphs: warmup, replay, and deterministic replay failure modes
- TensorRT-LLM vs vLLM: op fusion, padding-handling, and memory layout implications
- KV cache: eviction heuristics, prefix caching, and hit-rate analysis
- Batching strategy: dynamic batching vs constant slot pipelines
- Quantization fallbacks and per-layer perf/regression risks
- VPC/on-prem considerations: pinned memory limits, driver versions, and NCCL topology

Transcript:
00:00 Jordan: alright everyone thanks for carving out time today, um we wanted to focus on the more hairy parts of the runtime - kernel selection, cuda-graph stability, and actual tradeoffs we saw when running TRT-like fused kernels versus the vLLM approach.
00:18 Lisa: yeah this is perfect, we're seeing occasional spikes and one OOM last week with a 12k prompt test in our staging private cluster. we couldn't repro consistently, so grateful for the deep dive.
00:30 Priya: quick context - our tests on Redwood Dedicated showed that when the batch mix is heavy on long sequences the kernel picker tends to prefer fused TRT kernels for speed but that sometimes increases working set and triggers eviction. we think there's interplay with the cuda-graph warm path.
00:45 Arjun: can you unpack 'kernel picker' a bit? is that runtime decided or compile-time? we've seen differences depending on driver and cuda version.
00:54 Priya: good Q. the picker is dynamic - it consults model profile (layer shapes, self-attention dims), sequence length histogram, and available device memory. it tries to pick the kernel variant that minimizes per-token latency while keeping peak memory under the SLO. but on cold path where cuda-graphs are captured, the graph can bake in certain buffer allocations which then cause fragmentation on heterogeneous workloads.
01:20 Sofia: to add, TRT-LLM style kernels often fuse attention + ffw, which reduces kernel launch overhead, but increases the working buffer footprint. vLLM-style tends to be more modular (more smaller kernels), which is sometimes friendlier to huge-kv-cache workloads because it streams and reuses smaller buffers.
01:40 Emily: so vLLM is, uh, less memory hungry? seems odd given more kernels = more overhead.
01:46 Priya: it depends - modular kernels let you keep certain KV cache buffers on pinned host memory and page in/out smaller allocations. fused kernels might keep large temp tensors on device which increases fragmentation and makes CUDA graph replay brittle.
02:05 Samir: this matches our incident. we saw fragmentation over days, memory climbed intermittently and then next giant request failed. surfacing memory defrag metrics would help.
02:15 Jordan: action item - Priya will run a fragmentation profiler and share patterns.

(roughly 10m of detailed profiling discussion where attendees share traces)

10:20 Priya: here's an odd one - when we snapshot cuda graphs with TRT fused ops on A100 with driver 535.x, the replay path would sometimes hit a kernel variant that expects different workspace alignment, leading to non-deterministic OOMs. it's a mix of JIT variants and alignment assumptions.
10:40 Arjun: we run different minor driver patches across our fleet - could that be the root cause?
10:45 Priya: yes, totally. one of our reproducible cases was fixed by standardizing on 535.107 versus 535.92. recommended to pin driver + cuDNN versions in private deployments.
11:02 Lisa: are there perf regressions if we force the runtime off fused kernels?
11:10 Marco: small regressive hit in p95 latency (~7-12%) on short sequences, but for long sequences throughput sometimes improves because you avoid large temporary allocations and you get higher sustained concurrency. it's workload dependent.
11:30 Priya: also worth noting cache hit rates matter: if you get high KV cache hits then fused kernels shine because reduced memory traffic; if you're doing a lot of generation from scratch the modular path is more predictable.

18:00 Lisa: the KV cache eviction policy - you mentioned LRU-ish with pinning for hot prefixes?
18:06 Priya: correct. we use a weighted-LRU tuned by prefix frequency and model route pin list. in Dedicated we give customers control to pin explicit keys. this helps interactive apps. but if lots of clients pin big prefixes that drives fragmentation.
18:28 Arjun: can we log KV key sizes and eviction events to a central place?
18:33 Jordan: yes we can emit eviction traces to console / s3 and ship a small CSV. Priya will share the format.

22:15 Priya: about batching - we saw big differences between dynamic micro-batching and a slot-based batching approach. slot batching guarantees memory per slot which reduces jitter and is friendlier to cuda-graph capture, but it's less efficient if you have lots of tiny one-offs. dynamic batching is more efficient average cost but creates variable memory pressure spikes.
22:45 Emily: for us predictability > raw average cost - we'd prefer p99 guarantees.
22:50 Marco: then slot batching with conservative per-slot reservation plus overflow dynamic queue is a good hybrid. we can show config that Redwood Optimize recommends.

28:30 Priya: quantization - INT8 fused kernels in TRT can give big cost wins, but we saw layerwise quality regressions if fallback to fp16 isn't smooth. important to have per-layer calibration and an automatic regression monitor.
28:50 Lisa: do you ship calibration artifacts?
28:55 Priya: yes we can export calibration tables and we recommend per-customer calibration pass on representative datasets. Marco: and on private deployments, keep an automated rollback if eval metrics on prompt-set drift beyond tolerance.

33:10 Arjun: VPC/on-prem differences - any gotchas? we ran into NCCL topologies causing slow all-reduce on multi-gpu nodes during beam search.
33:20 Sofia: two things - ensure IB/mellanox firmware + driver alignment and isolate control plane traffic; also pinned host memory quotas in some enterprise kernels need bumping for large KV cache.
33:40 Samir: we have strict security - do these changes require host kernel modules or elevated privileges?
33:46 Marco: nothing kernel-level beyond standard NV driver, but some profiling tools need sudo for perf counters. for managed Dedicated we handle that; for private we provide a checklist.

40:05 Lisa: can Redwood run a canary on a Dedicated pool for us with our dataset? we'd like end-to-end validation - perf, L2/regression, and stability over 72h.
40:12 Jordan: yes - we propose a 72h canary with two kernel strategies: force-TTR-fused and modular-vLLM, plus slot-batching config. we'll run both and compare p50/p90/p99, memory drift, eviction counts.
40:30 Priya: we'll also run a CUDA-graph stress sweep: capture graphs at T0, apply jittered workloads, replay, and check deterministic allocations. will test across driver versions.
40:45 Lisa: perfect. can you also include the quantization regression guardrails?
40:52 Marco: included. we'll run INT8 with per-layer fallback and export metrics for automatic rollback threshold.

47:00 (discussion of instrumentation and logs)
47:15 Priya: sample artifacts we'll share - lightweight cuda-graph capture script (bash+python), fragmentation profiler (summaries of malloc/free patterns), and a benchmark sheet with plotting; sending links after the call.
47:33 Jordan: note - security docs and SOC2 appendix were requested earlier; we will send the compliance bundle for Private deployment.

55:10 Emily: timeline wise, if we get those artifacts and run the canary, we'd like a proposal to convert a small fleet to Dedicated in Q4.
55:18 Jordan: understood - we'll aim to have the proposal and cost model after the canary analysis (3-5 business days post-run).
